title: Phone Calls in Spanish: How to Answer, Ask and Hang Up

meta_description: Phone calls in Spanish: answering with ¿Diga?, ¿Bueno? or ¿Aló?, asking for someone, leaving messages, bad connections, formal calls and hanging up politely.
excerpt: ¿Diga?, ¿Bueno?, ¿Aló?: everything you need to survive a phone call in Spanish.

body_html:
Phone calls in Spanish are a challenge even for confident learners, because you can’t see faces or gestures, the line may be poor, and people speak fast. The good news is that phone conversations follow predictable patterns. Learn how people answer in different countries, how to ask for someone, what to say when the line is bad and how to end the call, and you’ll handle most calls with confidence, from booking a table to talking to a colleague.

Key takeaways
  • People answer with ¿Diga? or ¿Sí? (Spain), ¿Bueno? (Mexico) and ¿Aló? (much of South America).
  • Ask for someone with ¿Está Ana? or ¿Podría hablar con…?
  • Bad line: No te oigo bien. Se corta.
  • End politely: Bueno, te dejo. ¡Hasta luego!
{{toc}}

Answering phone calls in Spanish

CountryCommon greeting
Spain¿Diga? / ¿Dígame? / ¿Sí?
Mexico¿Bueno?
Colombia, Peru, Chile, Venezuela¿Aló?
Argentina, Uruguay¿Hola?
Businesses everywhereBuenos días, [empresa], ¿en qué puedo ayudarle?

The RAE dictionary lists diga and dígame as the expressions used in Spain to answer the phone.

Calling and asking for someone

  • Hola, soy Laura. ¿Está Carlos? Hi, it’s Laura. Is Carlos there?
  • ¿Podría hablar con la señora Gómez, por favor? Could I speak to Mrs Gómez, please?
  • Llamo por el anuncio del departamento. I’m calling about the apartment ad.
  • ¿De parte de quién? Who’s calling? (they ask you)
  • Un momento, ahorita se lo paso. One moment, I’ll put him on.
  • No está en este momento. ¿Quiere dejarle un recado? He’s not here right now. Would you like to leave a message?

Leaving a message

  • ¿Le puede decir que me llame? Can you ask him to call me?
  • Mi número es el 612 345 678. My number is 612 345 678.
  • Hola, soy Tom. Te llamaba para… Llámame cuando puedas. Hi, it’s Tom. I was calling to… Call me when you can. (voicemail)

Phone numbers are often read in pairs: seis doce, treinta y cuatro, cincuenta y seis…

{{image:2}}

Bad connections

  • No te oigo bien. I can’t hear you well.
  • Se corta. It’s cutting out.
  • ¿Me oyes? Can you hear me?
  • Tengo poca cobertura. I have bad signal.
  • Te llamo en cinco minutos. I’ll call you back in five minutes.
  • ¿Puedes repetirlo más despacio, por favor? Can you repeat that more slowly, please?

Hearing vs listening on the phone: see {{link:oir-vs-escuchar|oír vs escuchar}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Formal and business calls

For formal calls, use usted and polite conditionals: Buenos días, le llamo de parte de la empresa X (Good morning, I’m calling on behalf of company X), Quería consultar una duda sobre mi factura (I wanted to ask about my bill), ¿Me podría pasar con el departamento de reclamaciones? (Could you put me through to the complaints department?). Before an important call, write down the key vocabulary and a couple of sentences explaining why you’re calling. Asking someone to spell a name is common: ¿Me lo puede deletrear? For written follow-ups, see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.

Ending the call

  • Bueno, te dejo. Well, I’ll let you go.
  • Hablamos luego. Talk later.
  • Gracias por llamar. Thanks for calling.
  • Un beso, ¡chao! Kisses, bye! (friends and family)
  • Muchas gracias, que tenga un buen día. Thank you very much, have a good day. (formal)

A sample call

  • Restaurant: Restaurante La Plaza, buenas tardes.
  • You: Hola, buenas tardes. Quería reservar una mesa para cuatro el sábado a las nueve. (Hello, good afternoon. I’d like to book a table for four on Saturday at nine.)
  • Restaurant: Perfecto. ¿A nombre de quién? (Perfect. Under what name?)
  • You: De Tom Clark. ¿Se lo deletreo? (Tom Clark. Shall I spell it?)
  • Restaurant: Sí, por favor.

Tips for understanding

Phone Spanish is harder because you lose visual clues and audio quality drops. Don’t be shy about saying Perdone, mi español no es perfecto. ¿Puede hablar un poco más despacio? (Sorry, my Spanish isn’t perfect. Could you speak a bit more slowly?). Most people will gladly adapt. Practice with podcasts and voice notes from friends, which train your ear for audio-only Spanish; I explain why listening practice works in {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}.

Calls with friends and family

Informal calls are warmer and more relaxed. Friends often open with ¡Hola! ¿Qué onda? ¿Puedes hablar? (Hi! How are you? Is this a good time?) or ¿Estás ocupado? (Are you busy?). Family calls may end with a long series of goodbyes: Bueno, un beso. Dale un beso a los niños. Cuídate. ¡Chao, chao! Don’t be surprised if it takes a minute to actually hang up; it’s affectionate, not indecisive.

Voice notes

In many Spanish-speaking countries, voice notes (audios or notas de voz) are as common as calls. Friends send long audios instead of texting, and many people prefer them to answering the phone. They’re great listening practice, because you can replay them as often as you need. To reply, you might start with Hola, perdona que no te contesté antes… (Hi, sorry I didn’t answer earlier…). If you are calling a business, though, expect a menu first: Pulse uno para… (Press one for…), and be ready with your reference number: Mi número de cliente es…

Final thoughts

Know how people answer, how to ask for someone, what to say when the line drops and how to say goodbye. With these patterns, phone calls in Spanish become far less stressful. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you answer the phone in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Diga? or ¿Sí? in Spain, ¿Bueno? in Mexico, ¿Aló? in much of South America and ¿Hola? in Argentina.

faq.q: How do you ask for someone on the phone in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Está Carlos? (informal) or ¿Podría hablar con la señora Gómez? (formal).

faq.q: How do you say “the line is breaking up” in Spanish?
faq.a: Se corta, or No te oigo bien.
